title: The Man Who Stopped Time: Kingston to Kingston
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: The Boy of the Grain-Wharf: Kingston and the Crossing

stops.name: Kingston upon Thames: the birth of Edward Muggeridge
stops.campa: On 9 April 1830, in the market town of Kingston upon Thames, Edward James Muggeridge is born above the family grain-and-coal business on the river. His father John barges corn along the Thames; the boy grows among sacks and scales and the slow water. He is quick, restless, ambitious beyond the wharf. Later he will Saxon-spell himself Eadweard, reclaiming the old form carved on the Coronation Stone where Saxon kings were crowned in this very town, and take the surname Muybridge, the ancient one, he insists. The town that will bury him first sets him loose.
suggested_refs: The Coronation Stone, Kingston upon Thames

stops.name: New Orleans: the book agent lands in America
stops.campa: Around twenty, hungry for the New World, he sails for New York and enters the book trade. By January 1855 he has come down to New Orleans as a travelling book agent, carrying illustrated Shakespeares and fine bindings through a country still half wilderness. He is a salesman of images and words, an Englishman with a plan and an accent, working his way toward the golden coast where a new city is rising on the far Pacific. The tools of his second life, the printed picture, the sequence of plates, are already in his hands.
suggested_refs: Illustrated editions of Shakespeare, mid-19th c.

stops.name: San Francisco: Muygridge, bookseller of Montgomery Street
stops.campa: By 1856 he has settled in booming San Francisco and set up as a bookseller on Montgomery Street, agent for the London Printing and Publishing Company. He sells engravings and lithographs to a gold-rush city that wants pictures of the wider world. He is prosperous, dapper, known about town. He has not yet touched a camera. Then, in the spring of 1860, he sells the business to his brother, means to sail home to England to buy stock, and takes the overland stage east across the continent. The road to Fort Smith will change everything.
stops.quote: I have this day sold to my brother, Thomas S. Muybridge
stops.quote_source: Notice in the San Francisco Bulletin, May 1860
suggested_refs: Muybridge bookshop notices, San Francisco Bulletin, 1860

segments.name: The Blow to the Head: the Stagecoach and the Remaking

stops.name: North of Fort Worth, Texas: the runaway stagecoach
stops.campa: On 22 July 1860, on the Butterfield Overland Mail road above Fort Worth, the horses of the Concord stage bolt and cannot be held. The coach smashes into a tree; the driver and one passenger are killed outright, the rest flung and broken. Muybridge is thrown headlong and strikes his skull against a rock. Everything goes dark. In this instant, the tradition holds, a tradesman dies and an artist is born: the injury that will loose the strange, obsessive, brilliant man who chases the invisible instant. Motion has nearly killed him. He will spend his life arresting it.
suggested_refs: Butterfield Overland Mail route markers, Texas

stops.name: Fort Smith, Arkansas: waking with nine days lost
stops.campa: He wakes in a hospital bed at Fort Smith with no memory of the nine days since he ate supper at a wayside cabin 150 miles back. His head splits; his vision is doubled, his hearing dimmed, taste and smell gone, his mind confused. It is said his black hair turns grey in three days. The physicians can do little on the frontier. The change is not only physical: those who knew the smooth bookseller find him afterward eccentric, risk-taking, prone to rages and to genius; a different man walks out of Fort Smith than the one the coach threw down.

stops.name: London: Sir William Gull and the years of shadow
stops.campa: He returns to England to heal, and is treated by Sir William Gull, physician to the Queen's household, who advises open air, riding, and no strain. For several years Muybridge nearly vanishes from the record: Paris, patents, small inventions, a washing machine, a printing plate. Somewhere in this shadow-time he learns the wet-collodion craft of photography, the sun-drawing that will be his instrument. When he steps back into the light in San Francisco he is no longer Muggeridge the bookseller. He signs his negatives with the name of the sun.

segments.name: Helios: the Flying Studio and the Great Views

stops.name: San Francisco: the return of Helios, sun-drawer
stops.campa: On 13 February 1867 Muybridge is back in San Francisco, reborn as a photographer under the pseudonym Helios, the Greek sun, for photography is drawing with light. He builds a portable darkroom into a light two-wheeled carriage and paints on its back the name Helios' Flying Studio. With it he can carry the chemistry of the wet plate into any wilderness, coating, exposing, and developing before the collodion dries. The instant he once nearly died beneath, he will now hunt and pin to glass. The man who lost nine days sets out to capture single seconds.

stops.name: Yosemite Valley: the first great views, 1867
stops.campa: From June to November 1867 Helios climbs into Yosemite and makes seventy-two large views and more than a hundred stereographs of the cathedral valley: Yosemite Falls thundering, El Capitan's sheer face, the Merced mirror-still. He lashes himself to the edges of cliffs for the vantage; he waits on the light. The prints astonish San Francisco and make his name overnight. Where Carleton Watkins had gone before, Muybridge goes higher, stranger, more dramatic: inventing clouds later in the darkroom, arranging the sublime. The wilderness photographer is the same eye that will later dissect a stride.

stops.name: Sitka, Alaska: photographing the new Territory
stops.campa: In 1868, the year after the purchase of Alaska, the United States government sends Muybridge north to photograph the newly acquired Territory. He sails to Sitka and the Alexander Archipelago, documenting the fortress-town, the rain-forest coast, the totems and houses of the Tlingit. His views of Alaska help fix the far corner of the young continent in the American imagination. The camera that will one day map the geometry of a running body first maps the edges of an empire: glaciers, harbors, the last frontier of the sun's drawing.

stops.name: Point Reyes: the lighthouses of the Pacific coast
stops.campa: In 1871 the United States Lighthouse Board commissions Muybridge to photograph the beacons of the Pacific coast, from the fog-wrapped tower at Point Reyes to the lights of the Farallones and the Oregon shore. He records the lonely lamps that guard the shipping lanes, the keepers, the surf below sheer bluffs. The same year, on 20 May, he marries Flora Shallcross Stone, a divorcée of twenty-one, half his age. Light and marriage arrive together. Both, in the years to come, will be undone: one lover, one bullet.

stops.name: Yosemite Valley: the mammoth plates of 1872
stops.campa: In 1872 Muybridge returns to Yosemite and makes fifty-one mammoth plates on 18-by-22-inch glass, the largest wilderness photographs yet attempted in America. He hauls the enormous cameras and the flying darkroom up to viewpoints no one has photographed, dangling over precipices, felling trees that block his sight-lines. The Bradley & Rulofson prints crown him the foremost landscape photographer of the West. In this same year Leland Stanford, railroad king and horseman, hears of the wizard who can make the sun obey, and sends for him with a question about a galloping horse.

segments.name: The Wager: Stanford's Question and the First Trials

stops.name: Sacramento: Stanford's question and the first trials, 1873
stops.campa: Leland Stanford, former governor, builder of the Central Pacific, breeder of trotters, poses in 1872 the question that will consume Muybridge: when a horse runs, is there an instant when all four hooves leave the ground together? No eye can settle it; the legs blur. Horsemen argue; Stanford, they say, has a wager on it. In 1873, at Union Park racetrack in Sacramento, Muybridge makes the first attempts, trying to freeze the trotter Occident with a single fast shutter against a white sheet. The images are faint ghosts, but they hint that the unsupported instant is real, and that the camera can prove it.
suggested_refs: Muybridge first Occident negatives, Union Park, Sacramento, 1873

stops.name: Lava Beds, Modoc War: the camera at the front
stops.campa: In the spring of 1873 Muybridge carries his flying studio to the Modoc War in the volcanic lava beds of northern California, where Captain Jack's band holds the black stone fortress against the U.S. Army. He photographs the soldiers, the Warm Springs scouts, the desolate battlefield of cinders. These are among the first photographs made near an active American Indian war. Between the horse trials, the artist of arrested motion turns his lens on history caught mid-stride: an army bogged in lava, a people at the end of their ground.
suggested_refs: Lava Beds National Monument, Captain Jack's Stronghold

segments.name: The Bullet: Larkyns, Calistoga, and the Napa Jury

stops.name: San Francisco: the discovery in the photographer's house
stops.campa: In October 1874 Muybridge finds, tucked with a photograph of his infant son Florado, a note in Flora's hand and the child's name written as 'Little Harry.' He confronts the midwife, who lets slip that the drama critic Major Harry Larkyns, charming, penniless, a fixture of the theatres, has been the young wife's lover, and may be the boy's true father. The betrayed husband, already a man remade by a blow to the skull, goes cold and deliberate. He takes his revolver, learns where Larkyns is, and boards the boat north. He tells no one to stop him.
suggested_refs: Photograph of Florado Helios Muybridge, infant

stops.name: Yellow Jacket Mine, near Calistoga: the killing of Harry Larkyns
stops.campa: On the night of 17 October 1874 Muybridge comes by wagon and ferry to the Yellow Jacket quicksilver mine above Calistoga, where Larkyns is surveying. He knocks; a card game is in progress; Larkyns comes to the door. Muybridge speaks, then fires a single ball point-blank into the heart. Larkyns staggers out under an oak and dies within minutes. The photographer does not flee. He sits calmly among the horrified miners, tells them plainly that he has killed the man who wronged him, that men of family will understand, and that he has no regret. He waits to be taken.
stops.quote: Good evening, Major, my name is Muybridge, and here's the answer to the letter you sent my wife.
stops.quote_source: Muybridge to Harry Larkyns at the Yellow Jacket Mine, as recorded in trial testimony and biographies
suggested_refs: Yellow Jacket Mine site, near Calistoga
Contemporary newspaper accounts of the Larkyns killing

stops.name: Napa Courthouse: acquitted by justifiable homicide, February 1875
stops.campa: In February 1875 Muybridge stands trial for murder at the Napa County courthouse before Judge W. W. Wallace. His counsel does not much deny the deed; he pleads the outrage of a wronged husband. Stanford quietly helps pay the defense. The judge instructs the all-male jury that the law knows no such excuse. They deliberate through the night and return, against his instruction, a verdict of not guilty: justifiable homicide. They cannot punish, they say, a man for doing what any of them would have done. At the words Muybridge breaks: he sobs, convulses, and collapses. A free man, he is spirited out of California toward the tropics.
stops.quote: If their verdict was not in accordance with the law, it was in accordance with the law of human nature.
stops.quote_source: Contemporary account of the Napa jury's reasoning, February 1875

segments.name: The Tropics of Exile: Panama and the Coffee Coast

stops.name: Panama City: the Pacific Mail exile begins
stops.campa: In February 1875, days after his acquittal, Muybridge boards a Pacific Mail steamer and leaves the scene of his ruin for a nine-month commission in Central America. He lands at the Isthmus of Panama, photographing the port, the railway across the neck of the continent, the churches and jungle of the tropics for the steamship company, which wants his pictures to lure trade and settlers. Wifeless: Flora will die that July, her small son sent to an orphanage. The exile buries himself in work, coating plates in tropical heat, inventing skies for volcanoes back home.

stops.name: Antigua, Guatemala: the coffee plantations and the volcanoes
stops.campa: For six months Muybridge works in Guatemala, his richest tropical ground, based near Antigua beneath its ring of volcanoes. He photographs the colonial ruins, the indigenous coffee-pickers of Las Nubes, the weeding and drying of the beans, the cochineal cactus, whole villages posed among the drying-yards: a portrait of an emerging coffee empire built for its investors. Back in San Francisco he will deepen these prints, painting in moonlight and cloud. Only five copies of the great album are made. Renewed, his grief worked into labor, he sails home to California and to the horse still waiting on the Palo Alto track.
suggested_refs: Muybridge, 'The Pacific Coast of Central America... and the Cultivation and Shipment of Coffee' (1876)
Village of coffee pickers at Las Nubes, Muybridge

segments.name: The Wager Settled: Palo Alto and the Horse in the Air

stops.name: Palo Alto Stock Farm: the bank of cameras, 15 June 1878
stops.campa: On 15 June 1878, before invited turfmen and the press at Stanford's Palo Alto farm, the great experiment succeeds. Along the track a bank of twenty-four cameras faces a white wall marked in numbered lines. Threads stretched across the course run to electric shutters; as the racing mare Sallie Gardner strikes each trip-wire, the circuit breaks and the shutter fires, one after another, in a thousandth of a second. Developed on the spot, the plates show what no eye ever saw: the galloping horse, at full stretch, all four hooves gathered clear of the earth. The wager is settled. Motion has been arrested and read.
stops.quote: The Horse in Motion. 'Sallie Gardner,' owned by Leland Stanford; running at a 1.40 gait over the Palo Alto track, 19th June 1878.
stops.quote_source: Muybridge, caption to the published cabinet-card series, 1878
suggested_refs: 'The Horse in Motion' (Sallie Gardner at a Gallop), Muybridge 1878

segments.name: The Ghost of Cinema: the Wheel of Life and the Atlas of Bodies

stops.name: San Francisco: the zoopraxiscope whirls the frozen frames to life
stops.campa: Having stopped motion, Muybridge now gives it back. In 1879 he devises the zoopraxiscope: a lantern that spins a glass disc painted with his sequenced figures past a slotted counter-wheel, so the still phases blur into one moving image thrown on a wall. On 4 May 1880, before the San Francisco Art Association, the horse gallops again on the screen; a bull charges, an athlete runs, from images built out of dead instants. The audience sees the first projected moving pictures in history. The ghost of cinema is loosed. The man who arrested the second has invented the illusion that will fill the coming century's dark theatres.

stops.name: Paris: Marey's soirée and the meeting of the motion-hunters
stops.campa: On 26 September 1881 the physiologist Étienne-Jules Marey gathers the science of Paris into his apartment at 11 Boulevard Delessert, below the Trocadéro, to meet the American who has caught the horse in the air. Muybridge whirls his zoopraxiscope before Helmholtz and the men of the laboratories; days later the painter Meissonier fills his studio on the Boulevard Malesherbes with artists to see the same marvel. Here two obsessions fuse: Muybridge, who reads the body with banks of cameras, and Marey, who will read it with a single chronophotographic gun. From this room the study of motion becomes a science, and the road runs toward the moving film.
suggested_refs: Meissonier's studio soirée for Muybridge, Boulevard Malesherbes

stops.name: Royal Institution, London: the sun-picture lecture, 1882
stops.campa: In 1882 Muybridge crosses to Europe and lectures on the science of animal motion, whirling his zoopraxiscope before packed halls. At the Royal Institution in London he speaks to a sold-out audience that includes the Prince of Wales, the future Edward VII, and the great men of British science. But triumph curdles into feud: Stanford has published the horse studies under a hired doctor's name, all but erasing Muybridge, who sues and loses. The showman is celebrated across two continents and robbed of his own discovery in the same season.
suggested_refs: Stanford v. Muybridge dispute over 'The Horse in Motion' authorship

stops.name: University of Pennsylvania: the great atlas of Animal Locomotion
stops.campa: From 1884 the University of Pennsylvania, urged by the painter Thomas Eakins and Provost William Pepper, gives Muybridge an outdoor studio at Thirty-sixth and Pine and banks of cameras to record the moving body. For three years he photographs everything that walks, runs, climbs, falls, throws, lifts: horses, elephants, birds, and men and women, many nude, against his numbered grid. The result, published in 1887 as Animal Locomotion, is 781 collotype plates, over twenty thousand images: a vast, strange atlas of every gait of every creature, the body dissected into its hidden instants. It is the quipu's own dream: a gallery of moving bodies, motion itself made a book.
suggested_refs: Muybridge nude-figure locomotion plates, University of Pennsylvania

stops.name: Chicago, Midway Plaisance: the first movie theatre, 1893
stops.campa: At the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893, on the Midway Plaisance in Chicago, Muybridge opens the Zoopraxographical Hall: a building raised for the sole purpose of showing his moving pictures to a paying public. Night after night the crowds file in, pay their coin, and watch horses gallop and dancers whirl on the screen by lantern-light. It is the first commercial motion-picture theatre in the world, two years before the Lumières' Cinématographe. The old showman, sixty-three, stands in the doorway of the whole coming age of film: the movie house begins as his sideshow on the fairground midway.

segments.name: The Return to Kingston: the Lakes in the Garden

stops.name: Kingston upon Thames: the last years and the Great Lakes in the garden
stops.campa: In 1894 the old wanderer comes home for good to Kingston upon Thames, the grain-town of his birth, and lodges at last with his cousin Catherine Smith on Liverpool Road. He publishes his popular abridgements, Animals in Motion and The Human Figure in Motion, and lectures, and putters. In the back garden he sets about digging, at full scale of miniature, a working model of the Great Lakes of America, the continent that made him, carved into English soil. The man who mapped the far coasts and stopped the horse in mid-air ends as an eccentric old Englishman excavating a toy America in his cousin's yard.
suggested_refs: Muybridge, 'Animals in Motion' (1899) and 'The Human Figure in Motion' (1901)
BFI plaque, 2 Liverpool Road, Kingston upon Thames

stops.name: Kingston upon Thames: death, and the ashes at Woking
stops.campa: On 8 May 1904 Eadweard Muybridge dies of cancer at his cousin's house in Kingston, the town where he was born Edward Muggeridge seventy-four years before. The journey closes where it opened, Kingston to Kingston, the circle drawn. His body is cremated and the ashes laid in a grave at Woking, where the stonecutter, fittingly for a man who spent his life renaming himself, misspells him one final time as Eadweard Maybridge. He leaves his zoopraxiscope, his discs, and his plates to Kingston, and to the world the moving image: the horse forever in the air, the bodies forever walking.
